profile.feeling: Inside four walls, a city, a country – the most frequent preposition.

into, to (where to? + accusative: in die Stadt, ins Café)
in, within (time: in einer Stunde, im Mai)
in (a month, a season, a year, a week: im Mai, im Sommer, in diesem Jahr)

etymology.text: From Middle High German in, from Old High German in.

funFacts: German in and English in are one Germanic word, related to Greek ἐν (en) and Latin in.
pitfalls: Two-way preposition: Wo? → dative (Ich bin in der Küche), Wohin? → accusative (Ich gehe in die Küche).
in dem → im and in das → ins: Ich bin im Park. – not *in dem Park (unless “in that park”).
A city or a country without article: in Berlin, in Griechenland; with an article: in der Türkei, in der Schweiz.
Months and seasons take im (in + dem): im Mai, im Sommer; a year takes no preposition (2026) or im Jahr 2026 – not *in 2026.
subtleties: in for buildings you go inside (im Café, im Supermarkt); an open market or a square takes auf: auf dem Markt, auf dem Platz.

override.meaning: The concept gloss lists the examples “at home, at school”; Wiktionary glosses an as “at, upon, by, near, next to” (local) – the at-sense of a place.

senses.def: at, by, on (at an edge or side; where? + dative: am Fenster, an der Wand, am Bahnhof)
to, onto (where to? + accusative: ans Fenster, an die Wand)
on (days, parts of the day, dates: am Montag, am Abend, am 3. Mai – usually as am = an dem)
at (a school or university: an der Uni, an der Schule)

etymology.text: From Middle High German an(e), from Old High German ana, from Proto-West Germanic *ana, from Proto-Germanic *ana.

funFacts: an is the same word as English on and Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, on”).
pitfalls: an = at the side or edge (an der Wand, am Fenster); auf = on top of a surface (auf dem Tisch).
an dem → am, an das → ans: am Bahnhof, ans Meer.
Two-way preposition: Wo? + dative (am Fenster), Wohin? + accusative (ans Fenster).
Days, parts of the day and dates take an + dative, nearly always as am: am Montag, am Morgen, am Wochenende, am 3. Mai – but in der Nacht.
subtleties: “At” a place is three words in German: an (an edge: am Bahnhof), bei (a person or firm: beim Arzt) and in (inside: in der Schule).

override.meaning: The concept gloss lists the examples “at home, at school”; Wiktionary glosses bei as “(with a person, family, shop) at” – the at-sense of a place.

profile.feeling: At someone’s place – at the doctor’s, at grandma’s, at work.

senses.def: at (a person’s home, a shop, a doctor; a company: bei meiner Oma, beim Arzt, bei Siemens) + dative

examples.text: Ich bin heute bei meiner Oma.
examples.tr: Today I’m at my grandma’s.

examples.text: Mein Vater ist beim Arzt.

etymology.text: From Middle High German bī, from Old High German bī, from Proto-West Germanic *bī, from Proto-Germanic *bi. Compare English by.

funFacts: Like French chez, bei + a person means “at someone’s home”: bei Anna = chez Anna; Greek says στης Άννας.
pitfalls: bei is only for where you ARE: Ich bin bei meiner Mutter. Going there is zu: Ich gehe zu meiner Mutter (not *bei meiner Mutter gehen).
bei always takes the dative: bei dem → beim.
subtleties: bei uns can mean “at our home” or “in our country”: Bei uns isst man spät. (In our country people eat late.)

profile.feeling: Heading somewhere – to a person, to a building, to an event.

senses.def: to (a person, a building, an event; + dative: zum Arzt, zur Schule, zu meiner Oma)
at (in fixed phrases: zu Hause, zu Weihnachten)
to (before an infinitive: Ich habe keine Zeit zu kochen)

examples.text: Ich gehe zum Arzt.
examples.tr: I’m going to the doctor.

examples.text: Die Kinder gehen zur Schule.
examples.tr: The children go to school.

examples.text: Wir fahren zu meiner Tante.

examples.text: Der Kaffee ist zu heiß.
examples.tr: The coffee is too hot.

etymology.text: From a merger of Middle High German ze (Old High German za, zi) and zuo (Old High German zuo, from Proto-West Germanic *tō). Cognate with Dutch toe, English to, too.

funFacts: zu is English to and too – one German word does both jobs: zu Hause (at home), zu groß (too big).
pitfalls: zu always takes the dative, even for movement: zu dem Arzt → zum Arzt; zu der Post → zur Post.
zu Hause = at home (where), nach Hause = home (where to): Ich bin zu Hause. – Ich gehe nach Hause.
Cities and countries take nach, not zu: nach Berlin, nach Griechenland.
subtleties: zu is for going to a person or a place you visit for its purpose (zum Arzt, zur Post, zur Arbeit); in + accusative is for going inside (in die Küche, ins Kino).

profile.feeling: On the road to a city or a country – and home.

senses.def: to (cities, countries without article, directions, home: nach Berlin, nach Griechenland, nach links, nach Hause)
after (time and order, + dative: nach dem Essen, nach acht Uhr)

examples.text: Wir fliegen nach Athen.

examples.text: Der Zug fährt nach München.
examples.tr: The train goes to Munich.

examples.text: Nach dem Essen trinken wir Kaffee.
examples.tr: After the meal we drink coffee.

examples.text: Meiner Meinung nach ist das richtig.
examples.tr: In my opinion that’s right.

examples.text: Nach der Arbeit gehe ich nach Hause.
examples.tr: After work I go home.

profile.synonymsNone: A preposition has no true synonym; the neighbouring prepositions are compared in the pitfalls.

etymology.text: From Middle High German nāh, from Old High German nāh; related to nah (“near”). Cognate with Dutch na, English nigh.

funFacts: nach and nah (near) are one word historically – “going near” became “going to”.
pitfalls: nach for cities and countries WITHOUT article (nach Spanien); with an article use in + accusative: in die Türkei, in die Schweiz, in die USA.
nach is never used for going to a person or a building: zum Arzt, zur Schule (not *nach der Schule, which means “after school”).
Two meanings, both with the dative: nach Berlin / nach Hause (to) and nach dem Essen / nach der Arbeit (after).
subtleties: nach Hause has the old dative Hause; nach always takes the dative.
after + a verb is the conjunction nachdem (Nachdem ich gegessen habe, …); after = afterwards is danach.

profile.feeling: Coming out of something – a house, a cup, a country.

senses.def: from (origin: a country, a city; out of a place: aus Griechenland, aus dem Haus)
out of, made of (aus Holz = made of wood)
out of, for (a reason: aus Liebe)

examples.text: Er kommt gerade aus dem Haus.

examples.text: Der Tisch ist aus Holz.

etymology.text: From Middle High German ūȥ, from Old High German ūȥ (“out”), from Proto-West Germanic *ūt. Compare Dutch uit, English out.

funFacts: aus and English out are the same word – compare Der Ball ist im Aus (the ball is out) and Licht aus! (lights off!).
pitfalls: Origin is aus: Ich bin aus Griechenland. (not *von Griechenland)
aus always takes the dative: aus dem Haus, aus der Schule.
subtleties: aus = out of an inside (aus dem Haus, aus der Stadt); von = from a point, a person or the surface (vom Arzt, von der Arbeit).

profile.feeling: Starting point and owner: from a person, from work – and “of”.

senses.def: from (a person, a starting point: von meiner Mutter, von der Arbeit, vom Arzt)
of (owner, instead of the genitive: das Buch von meinem Bruder)
by (the doer in the passive: von Goethe geschrieben)
about, of (a topic: von etwas erzählen)

examples.text: Das Geschenk ist von meiner Mutter.
examples.tr: The present is from my mother.

examples.text: Er kommt gerade von der Arbeit.
examples.tr: He is just coming from work.

examples.text: Das ist das Auto von meinem Bruder.

collocations.tr: Who is it from? / Whose is it?

etymology.text: From Middle High German von(e) (“from”), from Old High German fon(a). Cognate with Old Dutch fan (modern van), Old Frisian fon, fan.

funFacts: von + dative is the everyday answer to wessen?: Wessen Buch ist das? – Von wem ist das Buch?
pitfalls: Origin of a person is aus, not von: Ich bin aus Athen. – von is for a starting point or a person (ein Brief von Anna).
von always takes the dative: von dem → vom.
subtleties: In speech von + dative replaces the genitive: das Auto von meinem Bruder = das Auto meines Bruders.
von in names (Johann Wolfgang von Goethe) is the noble particle, like Dutch van.

profile.feeling: Company and tools: with a friend, with milk, with the bus.

senses.def: with (together with; having: mit meinem Bruder, Tee mit Milch)
with, by (an instrument or transport: mit dem Messer, mit dem Bus)

examples.text: Ich trinke Tee mit Milch.
examples.tr: I drink tea with milk.

examples.text: Sie wohnt mit ihrer Schwester zusammen.

examples.text: Wir fahren mit dem Bus zur Schule.
examples.tr: We go to school by bus.

etymology.text: From Middle High German mite, mit, from Old High German miti, mit, from Proto-West Germanic *midi. Cognate with Middle English mid (“with”).

funFacts: mit is related to Greek μετά (metá, “with, among, after”) – the meta- of metaphor.
pitfalls: mit always takes the dative – also in the plural, where the noun adds -n: mit meinen Brüdern, mit den Kindern.
Transport is mit + dative: mit dem Bus, mit dem Auto (not *mit Bus).
subtleties: mit as an adverb means “along, too”: Kommst du mit? (Are you coming along?)

senses.def: without (+ accusative: ohne Zucker, ohne meinen Bruder)

examples.text: Ohne dich gehe ich nicht.

examples.text: Er kommt ohne seinen Bruder.

etymology.text: From Middle High German āne, from Old High German āna, āno (“without”), from Proto-Germanic *ēnu, *ēnō. Possibly cognate with Ancient Greek ἄνευ (áneu, “without”).

funFacts: ohne may be a cousin of Greek ἄνευ – both mean “without”.
pitfalls: ohne takes the accusative: ohne meinen Bruder (not *ohne meinem Bruder).
No article is common: ohne Zucker, ohne Milch.
subtleties: Ohne mich! – a whole answer: “Count me out!”

profile.feeling: A present, a purpose, a person: this is for you.

senses.def: for (a person, a purpose, a price: für dich, für das Abendessen)
for, in favour of (für oder gegen)

examples.text: Bist du für oder gegen den Plan?

etymology.text: From Middle High German vür, from Old High German furi, from Proto-West Germanic *furi, from Proto-Germanic *furi. Historically interchangeable with vor; the split dates from the 18th century.

funFacts: Greek για covers both “for” and “about”; German splits them: für (for) and über (about).
pitfalls: für takes the accusative: für meinen Vater (masculine -en), für dich, für ihn.
A period of time often needs no für: Ich bleibe zwei Wochen (für zwei Wochen is also fine for a planned stay); a time still going on takes seit (S15).
subtleties: für vs vor: für = for; vor = in front of / before – they were once the same word.

profile.feeling: A topic you talk, read or write about – and above, over, across.

senses.def: about (a topic, + accusative: ein Buch über die Stadt)
over, above (Wo? + dative: Die Lampe hängt über dem Tisch.)
over, across (Wohin? + accusative: über die Straße)

examples.tr: That is a book about Greece.

examples.text: Wir sprechen über die Arbeit.
examples.tr: We’re talking about work.

examples.text: Die Lampe hängt über dem Tisch.
examples.tr: The lamp hangs above the table.

examples.text: Wir fahren über München nach Wien.
examples.tr: We’re going to Vienna via Munich.

etymology.text: From Middle High German über, from Old High German ubiri, ubari, from Proto-Germanic *ubiri, from Proto-Indo-European *upéri. Cognate with Ancient Greek ὑπέρ (hupér, “above”), Latin super, English over.

funFacts: über is Greek ὑπέρ (hupér) – the hyper- of hyperactive – and Latin super.
pitfalls: über meaning “about” always takes the accusative: über den Film, über die Stadt.
über = above without touching (Die Lampe ist über dem Tisch); auf = on, touching (Das Buch ist auf dem Tisch).
subtleties: über is a two-way preposition for place (S12): über dem Tisch (where) – über den Tisch (across, where to).

profile.feeling: Your own four walls – being at home, relaxed.

senses.def: at home, at ease (figurative: sich wie zu Hause fühlen)

examples.text: Ich bin heute zu Hause.
examples.tr: I’m at home today.

examples.text: Bist du zu Hause?
examples.tr: Are you at home?

examples.text: Fühl dich wie zu Hause!
examples.tr: Make yourself at home!

synonyms.nuance: at home – warm and homely; everyday word in southern Germany, Austria and Switzerland

etymology.text: From Middle High German ze hūse, from Old High German za hūse, zi hūse, equivalent to zu (“to”) + Hause, the old-fashioned dative of Haus (“house”).

funFacts: Russian splits it exactly like German: дома (at home) – домой (home, where to); Greek uses one phrase for both: στο σπίτι.
pitfalls: zu Hause = where (at home); nach Hause = where to (home): Ich bin zu Hause. – Ich will nach Hause.
Not *in Hause, *bei Hause, and not *zu Hause gehen.
subtleties: The -e of Hause is an old dative ending kept only in these phrases; elsewhere: im Haus.
The spelling zuhause (one word) is also accepted; das Zuhause is a noun: “home” as a place you belong to.

profile.feeling: The way home after a long day.

examples.text: Ich will nach Hause.
examples.tr: I want to go home.

examples.text: Wann kommst du nach Hause?
examples.tr: When are you coming home?

examples.text: Komm gut nach Hause!
examples.tr: Get home safely!

phrases.meaning: get home safely (said when someone leaves)

synonyms.nuance: home(wards) – common in southern German speech: Ich gehe heim.

etymology.text: From nach (“to”) + Hause, old dative of Haus (“house”).

funFacts: English “home” works without a preposition (go home) – German needs nach, Greek στο σπίτι, Turkish the dative eve.
pitfalls: nach Hause is movement (where to); being at home is zu Hause.
Not *zu Hause gehen: going home is always nach Hause gehen.
subtleties: The spelling nachhause (one word) is also accepted; nach Haus (without -e) is heard in speech and songs.

profile.feeling: School bags, the bell, the schoolyard – and the first day with a Schultüte.

senses.def: school (of thought, art: die Frankfurter Schule)

examples.text: Die Kinder sind in der Schule.
examples.tr: The children are at school.

examples.text: Meine Tochter geht schon zur Schule.
examples.tr: My daughter already goes to school.

examples.text: Nach der Schule essen wir zu Mittag.
examples.tr: After school we have lunch.

examples.text: Er gehört zur Frankfurter Schule.
examples.tr: He belongs to the Frankfurt School.

collocations.tr: to go to school, attend school

phrases.text: Nicht für die Schule, sondern für das Leben lernen wir.
phrases.tr: We learn not for school but for life.
phrases.meaning: learning is for life (a reversal of Seneca’s complaint “non vitae sed scholae discimus”)

etymology.text: From Middle High German schuole, from Old High German scuola, from Latin schola, from Ancient Greek σχολή (skholḗ, “leisure”).

funFacts: Greek σχολή first meant “leisure” – learning was what free people did with their free time; σχολείο and Schule are the same word.
On the first school day German children get a Schultüte, a big paper cone full of sweets.
pitfalls: in der Schule (at school – where) vs zur Schule / in die Schule (to school – where to).
False friend: das Gymnasium is an academic secondary school, not a gym.
subtleties: zur Schule gehen also means “to be a pupil”: Mein Sohn geht noch zur Schule.

profile.feeling: Lecture halls, libraries, student life.

examples.text: Sie studiert an der Universität Wien.
examples.tr: She studies at the University of Vienna.

examples.text: Die Universität ist sehr alt.
examples.tr: The university is very old.

examples.text: Die älteste Universität Deutschlands ist in Heidelberg.
examples.tr: The oldest university in Germany is in Heidelberg.

synonyms.nuance: any institution of higher education (also universities of applied sciences)

etymology.text: Borrowed from Latin ūniversitās (“the whole; a community, guild”). Compare Dutch universiteit.

funFacts: Heidelberg University, founded in 1386, is the oldest in present-day Germany.
Latin universitas meant a guild – the “whole body” of teachers and students.
pitfalls: an der Universität for studying or working there: Ich studiere an der Uni. – in der Universität only for being inside the building.
Stress on the last syllable: Uni-ver-si-TÄT; plural Universitäten.
subtleties: Students say Uni; Universität sounds official or written.

profile.feeling: Student life: lectures, the Mensa, friends.

examples.text: Ich bin heute an der Uni.
examples.tr: I’m at uni today.

examples.text: Nach der Uni gehen wir ins Café.
examples.tr: After uni we’re going to the café.

examples.text: Die Uni beginnt im Oktober.
examples.tr: The university term starts in October.

synonyms.nuance: institution of higher education in general

etymology.text: Clipping of Universität.

funFacts: German loves clipped words: die Uni, die Kita (Kindertagesstätte), der Prof, die Mensa (the university canteen, Latin “table”).
pitfalls: Plural with -s: die Unis (no -n in the dative: an den Unis).
subtleties: Uni is everyday speech, not slang – even professors say it.

profile.feeling: The daily grind – the job and the place you go to every morning.

senses.def: work, job; the workplace (bei der Arbeit, zur Arbeit)
a piece of work: a test at school, a paper (eine Arbeit schreiben)

examples.text: Mein Vater ist noch bei der Arbeit.
examples.tr: My father is still at work.

examples.text: Sie fährt jeden Tag mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.
examples.tr: She goes to work by bus every day.

examples.text: Ich suche Arbeit.
examples.tr: I’m looking for work.

examples.text: Morgen schreiben wir eine Arbeit in Mathe.
examples.tr: Tomorrow we’re writing a maths test.

phrases.text: Erst die Arbeit, dann das Vergnügen.

synonyms.nuance: a job – often a temporary or side job
a position, a post (eine Stelle suchen)

etymology.text: From Middle High German arbeit, from Old High German arbeit, from Proto-West Germanic *arbaiþi, from Proto-Germanic *arbaidiz, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃órbʰos (“orphan, servant, slave”).

funFacts: Arbeit comes from the same root as Russian работа (rabota) – and “robot”, from Czech robota (forced labour).
pitfalls: At work = bei der Arbeit (colloquially auf der Arbeit; in Austria and Bavaria also in der Arbeit); to work = zur Arbeit.
Plural Arbeiten only for pieces of work (Klassenarbeiten); “jobs” are Stellen or Jobs.
subtleties: die Arbeit is both the activity and the workplace: Ich habe viel Arbeit. – Ich bin bei der Arbeit.

profile.feeling: Desks, screens, coffee machine – nine to five.

senses.def: office (a room or building for desk work)

examples.text: Ich bin bis fünf im Büro.
examples.tr: I’m at the office until five.

examples.text: Mein Büro ist im dritten Stock.
examples.tr: My office is on the third floor.

examples.text: Wir buchen die Reise im Reisebüro.
examples.tr: We book the trip at the travel agency.

synonyms.nuance: working from home – a German pseudo-anglicism

etymology.text: From French bureau (“desk, office”), borrowed around 1700.

funFacts: Russian бюро and Turkish büro are the same French word; French bureau first meant a desk covered with coarse woollen cloth (bure).
pitfalls: Stress on the last syllable: Bü-RO; plural die Büros (with -s, so no -n in the dative: in den Büros).
subtleties: Homeoffice looks English but is German: in English you “work from home”.

profile.feeling: Shop windows, opening hours – and the world of business deals.

senses.def: business (going to the toilet: sein Geschäft machen)

examples.text: Das Geschäft ist am Sonntag geschlossen.
examples.tr: The shop is closed on Sunday.

examples.text: Wir kaufen Wein in einem kleinen Geschäft.
examples.tr: We buy wine in a small shop.

examples.text: Das ist ein gutes Geschäft.
examples.tr: That’s a good deal.

phrases.meaning: in business there is no room for sentiment

synonyms.nuance: shop – a little more everyday, often a small shop
shop – anglicism, especially online shops and brand stores

etymology.text: From Middle High German gescheft, from Old High German giscaft, from Proto-West Germanic *gaskafti. Cognate with Yiddish געשעפֿט (gesheft).

funFacts: Geschäft is related to schaffen (to manage, to create): a Geschäft is “what one manages”.
pitfalls: das Geschäft is neuter (not *die).
Geschäft also means business: Wie gehen die Geschäfte? (How’s business?)
subtleties: Geschäft is the general word; Laden often sounds smaller and more everyday.

profile.feeling: The little shop on the corner that has everything.

senses.def: place, outfit, joint (a firm, a pub)

examples.text: Der Laden an der Ecke hat alles.
examples.tr: The shop on the corner has everything.

examples.text: Um acht macht der Laden zu.
examples.tr: The shop closes at eight.

examples.text: Mach bitte die Läden zu, es ist kalt.
examples.tr: Please close the shutters, it’s cold.

phrases.meaning: to run the whole show, to manage everything

etymology.text: From Middle High German laden, lade (“board; plank; shutter; shop”), from Old High German *lado. Probably akin to German Latte, English lath; unrelated to Lade.

funFacts: German shop-closing laws (Ladenschluss) keep most shops closed on Sundays.
pitfalls: der Laden (shop) vs laden (to load) – same spelling, different words.
Plural with umlaut: die Läden.
subtleties: In Middle High German laden meant a board or a shutter – and also the shop behind it.

profile.feeling: Trolleys, long shelves, the checkout queue.

examples.text: Ich kaufe Milch im Supermarkt.
examples.tr: I buy milk at the supermarket.

examples.text: Der Supermarkt ist bis 22 Uhr offen.
examples.tr: The supermarket is open until 10 p.m.

examples.text: Wo ist hier ein Supermarkt?
examples.tr: Where is there a supermarket around here?

etymology.text: From super- + Markt.

funFacts: The German discounters Aldi and Lidl have supermarkets all over Europe – Lidl also in Greece.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: die Supermärkte.
im Supermarkt (in a building) – but auf dem Markt (an open-air market).
subtleties: At German supermarket checkouts you pack your shopping yourself – and quickly.

profile.feeling: Stalls of fruit and flowers on the town square on Saturday morning.

examples.text: Samstags kaufen wir Obst auf dem Markt.
examples.tr: On Saturdays we buy fruit at the market.

examples.text: Der Käse ist vom Markt.
examples.tr: The cheese is from the market.

examples.text: Der Markt für Elektroautos wächst.
examples.tr: The market for electric cars is growing.

synonyms.nuance: bazaar – an oriental market or a charity sale

etymology.text: From Middle High German market, from Old High German marchat, from Proto-West Germanic *markat, from Latin mercātus (“trade, market”).

funFacts: German Christmas markets (the Nuremberg Christkindlesmarkt, the Dresden Striezelmarkt) are famous and copied around the world.
pitfalls: auf dem Markt (not *im Markt) for the open-air market; im Supermarkt for the shop.
Plural with umlaut: die Märkte.
subtleties: der Markt is also the economy: die Marktwirtschaft (market economy).

profile.feeling: A table for two, a menu, the bill at the end.

examples.text: Wir essen heute im Restaurant.
examples.tr: We’re eating at a restaurant today.

examples.text: Kennst du ein gutes griechisches Restaurant?
examples.tr: Do you know a good Greek restaurant?

examples.text: Das Restaurant ist am Montag geschlossen.
examples.tr: The restaurant is closed on Monday.

synonyms.nuance: a place to eat or drink
a traditional inn, especially in Bavaria and Austria

etymology.text: Borrowed from French restaurant, from restaurer (“to restore”): first a restoring broth, then the place that served it.

funFacts: Greek εστιατόριο and German Restaurant both name the place after what it does: εστιάζω (to feast), restaurer (to restore).
pitfalls: das Restaurant (neuter), plural die Restaurants.
Said the French way: the -ant is nasal, like in French.
subtleties: In Germany you usually wait to be seated only in better restaurants; in a pub you choose a free table.

profile.feeling: Coffee and cake in the afternoon – Kaffee und Kuchen.

examples.text: Wir trinken Kaffee im Café.
examples.tr: We drink coffee in the café.

examples.text: Das Café an der Ecke hat guten Kuchen.
examples.tr: The café on the corner has good cake.

examples.text: Treffen wir uns im Café?
examples.tr: Shall we meet at the café?

synonyms.nuance: coffee house – the word of Vienna’s classic cafés

etymology.text: Borrowed from French café. Doublet of Kaffee.

funFacts: Café and Kaffee go back to Ottoman Turkish kahve and Arabic قَهْوَة (qahwa).
pitfalls: das Café (the place) vs der Kaffee (the drink): different spelling, gender and stress – Ca-FÉ vs KAF-fee (in Austria Kaf-FEE).
Plural Cafés with -s.
subtleties: Many German cafés are also bakeries or cake shops (Konditorei); a Kneipe is a pub.

profile.feeling: Wards, nurses, visiting hours – a place you hope to leave soon.

examples.text: Meine Oma ist im Krankenhaus.
examples.tr: My grandma is in hospital.

examples.text: Der Krankenwagen fährt ins Krankenhaus.
examples.tr: The ambulance drives to the hospital.

examples.text: Sie arbeitet als Ärztin im Krankenhaus.
examples.tr: She works as a doctor in the hospital.

collocations.tr: to be in hospital (as a patient)

synonyms.nuance: hospital – the word in Austria and Switzerland
a large hospital, often a university hospital

etymology.text: From Kranker (“sick person, patient”) + -en- + Haus (“house”).

funFacts: Greek νοσοκομείο (“place for tending the sick”) and German Krankenhaus (“house of the sick”) are built on the same idea.
pitfalls: das Hospital exists but sounds old-fashioned; the normal word is Krankenhaus.
Plural with umlaut: die Krankenhäuser.
subtleties: im Krankenhaus liegen = to be in hospital as a patient; im Krankenhaus arbeiten = to work there.

profile.feeling: The red A sign on the street – medicines, advice, cough drops.

examples.text: Die Apotheke ist an der Ecke.
examples.tr: The pharmacy is on the corner.

examples.text: Ich hole Tabletten aus der Apotheke.
examples.tr: I’m getting tablets from the pharmacy.

examples.text: Welche Apotheke hat heute Notdienst?
examples.tr: Which pharmacy is on duty today?

collocations.tr: over the counter at the pharmacy

profile.synonymsNone: No everyday synonym: the shop with medicines is always die Apotheke (a Drogerie is a different shop).

etymology.text: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἀποθήκη (apothḗkē, “storehouse”). Doublet of Bodega, Bottich and Boutique.

funFacts: Russian аптека (apteka) is the same Greek word; Turkish says eczane.
pitfalls: False friend for Greeks: German Apotheke = pharmacy (φαρμακείο), not a storeroom (αποθήκη).
A Drogerie (dm, Rossmann) sells soap, cosmetics and household goods – medicines are in der Apotheke.
subtleties: German pharmacies take turns staying open at night and on Sundays (Notdienst); a sign on the door says which one is open.

profile.feeling: Accounts, cards and cash machines – or a bench in the park (plural Bänke).

examples.text: Ich muss noch zur Bank.
examples.tr: I still have to go to the bank.

examples.text: Er arbeitet bei einer Bank.
examples.tr: He works for a bank.

examples.text: Wir sitzen auf einer Bank im Park.
examples.tr: We’re sitting on a bench in the park.

collocations.tr: to get money from the bank

synonyms.nuance: savings bank – a public regional bank; many Germans simply say “zur Sparkasse”

etymology.text: From Old High German bank (“bench”); the money sense came in the 15th century after Italian banco, banca (“bench; money-changer’s table, bank”).

funFacts: Greek τράπεζα means both “table” and “bank” – just as the Italian banco (bench) that gave German Bank its money sense; English bankrupt is Italian banca rotta, “broken bench”.
pitfalls: Same singular, two plurals: die Banken (banks) – die Bänke (benches).
bei der Bank arbeiten = to work for a bank; zur Bank gehen = to go to the bank.
subtleties: In Germany many people still pay cash; the Sparkasse is in almost every town.

profile.feeling: Letters, parcels, stamps – the yellow sign of the post.

examples.text: Ich bringe das Paket zur Post.
examples.tr: I’m taking the parcel to the post office.

examples.text: Die Post ist neben dem Bahnhof.
examples.tr: The post office is next to the station.

examples.text: Ist heute Post für mich da?
examples.tr: Is there any post for me today?

collocations.tr: to go to the post office

synonyms.nuance: post-office branch – often inside another shop today

etymology.text: Borrowed from Italian posta, from posto, from Latin positus (“placed”).

funFacts: Latin posita “placed” refers to the relay stations along the road where fresh horses were placed for the messengers.
pitfalls: die Post means both the post office and the mail: Ich gehe zur Post. – Ich lese meine Post.
A job “post” is die Stelle, not die Post.
subtleties: Used in the singular; Postämter or Postfilialen when you count post offices.

profile.feeling: Platforms, announcements, a delayed train – and a meeting point.

senses.def: railway station, train station (also Busbahnhof = bus station)

examples.text: Wo ist der Bahnhof?
examples.tr: Where is the station?

examples.text: Wir treffen uns am Bahnhof.
examples.tr: Let’s meet at the station.

examples.text: Der Zug steht im Bahnhof.
examples.tr: The train is standing in the station.

phrases.meaning: I don’t understand a thing – it’s all Greek to me

synonyms.nuance: the main station of a city
a bus or tram stop – not a station

etymology.text: From Bahn (“track, railway”) + Hof (“yard, court”).

funFacts: Ich verstehe nur Bahnhof means “It’s all Greek to me”.
pitfalls: am Bahnhof = at the station (around it, meeting point); im Bahnhof = inside the station.
Plural with umlaut: die Bahnhöfe.
subtleties: A bus station is der Busbahnhof (ZOB); a stop is die Haltestelle.

profile.feeling: Departure boards, suitcases, goodbyes and hellos.

examples.text: Wir fahren zum Flughafen.
examples.tr: We’re going to the airport.

examples.text: Am Flughafen warten wir auf meine Tante.
examples.tr: At the airport we wait for my aunt.

examples.text: Der Flughafen ist weit von der Stadt.
examples.tr: The airport is far from the city.

etymology.text: From Flug (“flight”) + Hafen (“port”). Compare Icelandic flughöfn.

funFacts: The same picture in other languages: Greek αερολιμένας (air harbour), Turkish havalimanı (hava + liman), Russian аэропорт.
pitfalls: der Hafen is masculine, so der Flughafen; plural die Flughäfen.
At the airport = am Flughafen (not *im Flughafen, unless inside the building).
subtleties: Flughafen is literally “flight harbour”.

profile.feeling: Traffic, pavements, house numbers – and the street you live in.

examples.text: Die Kinder spielen auf der Straße.
examples.tr: The children are playing in the street.

examples.text: In welcher Straße wohnst du?
examples.tr: Which street do you live in?

examples.text: Die Straße ist sehr lang.
examples.tr: The street is very long.

collocations.tr: in the street, on the road

phrases.meaning: to be out of a job or without a home

synonyms.nuance: lane, small street – in Vienna the normal word for many streets

etymology.text: From Middle High German strāȥe, from Old High German strāȥa, from Proto-West Germanic *strātu, from Latin (via) strāta (“paved road”).

funFacts: Latin strata also gave English street, Italian strada – and colloquial Greek στράτα.
pitfalls: auf der Straße (on the open street) – but addresses use in: Ich wohne in der Goethestraße.
Written with ß in Germany and Austria; in Switzerland Strasse.
subtleties: auf der Straße stehen / sitzen can mean to be out of work or homeless.

profile.feeling: A town square with a fountain, cafés and pigeons.

examples.text: Das Café ist am Marktplatz.
examples.tr: The café is on the market square.

examples.text: Viele Leute sind auf dem Platz.
examples.tr: Many people are in the square.

examples.text: Hier ist kein Platz mehr.
examples.tr: There’s no more room here.

examples.text: Nehmen Sie bitte Platz!
examples.tr: Please take a seat!

synonyms.nuance: the market square, the main square of many German towns

etymology.text: From Middle High German plaz, from Old French place, from Latin platēa, from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa), short for πλατεῖα ὁδός (plateîa hodós, “broad way”). Cognate with English place.

funFacts: Platz is Greek πλατεία (square) – borrowed via Latin and French.
pitfalls: auf dem Platz (in the square), not *in dem Platz.
Platz also means space or seat: Wir haben keinen Platz. – Ist der Platz frei?
subtleties: Nehmen Sie Platz! is the polite “sit down”.

profile.feeling: Grass, trees, a bench, children playing – a Sunday walk.

examples.text: Die Kinder spielen im Park.
examples.tr: The children are playing in the park.

examples.text: Wir gehen im Park spazieren.
examples.tr: We’re going for a walk in the park.

examples.text: Der Englische Garten in München ist ein großer Park.
examples.tr: The English Garden in Munich is a big park.

collocations.tr: to go for a walk in the park

synonyms.nuance: garden – in names also a park: der Englische Garten

etymology.text: A doublet of inherited Pferch (“pen”); borrowed from Middle Dutch park and reinforced from French parc and English park in the 17th century.

funFacts: Munich’s Englischer Garten is bigger than New York’s Central Park.
pitfalls: Plural die Parks (no -n in the dative: in den Parks).
im Park (in dem Park): where? – in den Park: where to?
subtleties: Many German parks are called Garten: der Englische Garten (Munich), der Große Garten (Dresden).

profile.feeling: Streets, shops, noise – town life.

examples.text: Ich wohne in der Stadt.
examples.tr: I live in the city.

examples.text: Athen ist eine große Stadt.
examples.tr: Athens is a big city.

examples.text: Am Samstag fahren wir in die Stadt.
examples.tr: On Saturday we’re going into town.

phrases.meaning: medieval rule: a serf who lived in a town for a year and a day became free

etymology.text: From Middle High German stat, from Old High German stat, from Proto-West Germanic *stadi, from Proto-Germanic *stadiz, from Proto-Indo-European *stéh₂tis. Cognate with English stead.

funFacts: Stadt and English stead (instead, homestead) come from the same root as stehen (to stand): a town is “where one stands”.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: die Städte; dative plural den Städten.
German has one word for city and town: Stadt (Großstadt / Kleinstadt if needed).
subtleties: in die Stadt gehen often means “to go downtown”, even if you live in the city.

profile.feeling: A church, a few farms, everybody knows everybody.

examples.text: Meine Großeltern wohnen in einem kleinen Dorf.
examples.tr: My grandparents live in a small village.

examples.text: Im Dorf kennt jeder jeden.
examples.tr: In the village everybody knows everybody.

examples.text: Das Dorf hat nur eine Straße.
examples.tr: The village has only one street.

collocations.tr: to live in the country, in a village

phrases.text: Das sind für mich böhmische Dörfer.
phrases.tr: Those are Bohemian villages to me.
phrases.meaning: I don’t understand any of it – it’s all Greek to me

etymology.text: From Middle High German dorf, from Old High German dorf, thorph, from Proto-West Germanic *þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą. Cognate with Dutch dorp, Old English þorp.

funFacts: English place names in -thorpe (Scunthorpe) contain the same word as Dorf.
pitfalls: Plural with umlaut: die Dörfer, dative den Dörfern.
auf dem Dorf (village life, in the country) vs im Dorf (inside the village).
subtleties: Dorf can be figurative: Berlin ist doch ein Dorf! (everyone knows each other).

profile.feeling: Borders, flags – and the green countryside.

examples.text: Griechenland ist ein schönes Land.
examples.tr: Greece is a beautiful country.

examples.text: Aus welchem Land kommst du?
examples.tr: Which country do you come from?

examples.text: Wir wohnen auf dem Land.
examples.tr: We live in the countryside.

examples.text: Bayern ist ein Bundesland.
examples.tr: Bavaria is a federal state.

phrases.meaning: customs differ from place to place – when in Rome, do as the Romans do

synonyms.nuance: the state as a political body

etymology.text: From Middle High German lant, from Old High German lant, from Proto-West Germanic *land, from Proto-Germanic *landą, from Proto-Indo-European *lendʰ- (“land, heath”). Compare Dutch, English and Danish land.

funFacts: Germans call Greece Griechenland after the Latin Graeci; Greeks call it Ελλάδα, and Turks Yunanistan (from Ionia).
pitfalls: Country names in -land are neuter and take no article: in Griechenland, nach Deutschland. With an article: die Türkei, die Schweiz → in der Türkei, in die Türkei.
auf dem Land = in the countryside, not “on the country”.
subtleties: Plural die Länder; the poetic plural Lande survives in phrases like in deutschen Landen.
